In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the retention of BSA is mainly determined by charge of the protein, and that the retention of immune complexes is low in hyaline cartilage.
the penetration of cationic proteins into the cartilage is not a species-specific phenomenon, and that the penetration is not restricted to immune complexes but also occurs with native proteins.
the charge of the antigen plays a more important role for antigen retention than the immune complex formation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
cationization of proteins is a useful technique for the delivery of proteins into articular cartilage, and that this is not restricted to murine cartilage.

cationized BSA is a useful model antigen for studying the retention of antigens in articular cartilage, and that cationized protein is a useful model for studying the penetration of antigens in cartilage.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the electrical charge of a protein is the major determinant for its penetration in hyaline cartilage.
the retention of cationic proteins in cartilage is considerably higher than that of anionic proteins.
cationized BSA binds to cartilage in a much more effective manner, which is important in the context of arthritis.
